chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddaq ibn Sadaqa, from Ammar ibn Musa, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about the Aqeeqa for the newborn, how it is? He said: When seven days come upon the newborn, name him by the name that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has named him with. Then shave his head, and give in charity the weight of his hair in gold or silver, and slaughter a ram for him. And if a ram is not found, suffice it with whatever suffices in the Udhiyah (Qurbani), or else a lamb, the largest of the lambs of the year. And give the midwife a quarter of it. And if there is no midwife, it is for his mother; she gives it to whomever she wishes, and feeds from it ten of the Muslims. If they increase, that is better, and eat from it.

And the Aqeeqa is obligatory whether one is rich or poor, when one is able. And if one does not perform the Aqeeqa for him until he performs the Udhiyah for him, then the Udhiyah suffices for him. And he said: If the midwife is a Jewess, who does not eat from the slaughter of the Muslims, she is given the value of a quarter of the ram.

key_terms.الْأُضْحِيَّة: Udhiyah: The sacrifice offered during Eid al-Adha
key_terms.الْعَقِيقَةُ: Aqeeqa: The sacrifice made for a newborn child on the seventh day
key_terms.رُبُعُهَا: A quarter of the sacrificed animal

ai.seo_question: What are the steps and rulings for performing Aqeeqa for a newborn in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi establishes the Aqeeqa as a recommended act (mustahabb) that becomes obligatory upon wealth accumulation, detailing the specific rituals of naming, shaving, and sacrificing a ram on the seventh day. It provides practical jurisprudential nuances, such as substituting a lamb if a ram is unavailable and adjusting compensation for non-Muslim midwives, reflecting the flexibility within Shia fiqh. The text underscores the social dimension of the ritual by mandating the distribution of meat to ten Muslims, thereby fostering community bonds alongside the spiritual act of gratitude.
